claim: Binding of the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) to origins of replication marks the first step in the initiation of replication of the genome in all eukaryotic cells.
source: Binding of the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) to origins of replication marks the first step in the initiation of replication of the genome in all eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ORC function in eukaryotic DNA replication.

claim: The structure of the active form of human ORC was determined by X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we report the structure of the active form of human ORC determined by X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methods used to determine the structure.

claim: The human ORC complex is composed of an ORC1/4/5 motor module lobe in an organization reminiscent of the DNA polymerase clamp loader complexes.
source: The complex is composed of an ORC1/4/5 motor module lobe in an organization reminiscent of the DNA polymerase clamp loader complexes.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: A second lobe of the human ORC complex contains the ORC2/3 subunits.
source: A second lobe contains the ORC2/3 subunits.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: The human ORC complex is organized as a double-layered shallow corkscrew, with the AAA+ and AAA+-like domains forming one layer, and the winged-helix domains (WHDs) forming a top layer.
source: The complex is organized as a double-layered shallow corkscrew, with the AAA+ and AAA+-like domains forming one layer, and the winged-helix domains (WHDs) forming a top layer.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: CDC6 fits easily between ORC1 and ORC2, completing the ring and the DNA-binding channel, forming an additional ATP hydrolysis site.
source: CDC6 fits easily between ORC1 and ORC2, completing the ring and the DNA-binding channel, forming an additional ATP hydrolysis site.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling of CDC6 into the ORC structure.

claim: Analysis of the ATPase activity of the complex provides a basis for understanding ORC activity as well as molecular defects observed in Meier-Gorlin Syndrome mutations.
source: Analysis of the ATPase activity of the complex provides a basis for understanding ORC activity as well as molecular defects observed in Meier-Gorlin Syndrome mutations.
evidence: This is based on biochemical assays performed on wild-type and mutant ORC complexes.

claim: ORC and CDC6 function as an ATP-dependent assembler that first recruits a ring-shaped MCM2-7 hexamer with bound Cdt1 to DNA.
source: ORC and CDC6 then function as an ATP-dependent assembler that first recruits a ring-shaped MCM2-7 hexamer with bound Cdt1 to DNA, and then loads a second MCM2-7 hexamer in a head-to-head orientation, whereby this double hexamer is topologically linked to double-stranded DNA (reviewed in [O'Donnell et al., 2013; Siddiqui et al., 2013; Bell and Labib, 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: ORC and CDC6 load a second MCM2-7 hexamer in a head-to-head orientation, whereby this double hexamer is topologically linked to double-stranded DNA.
source: ORC and CDC6 then function as an ATP-dependent assembler that first recruits a ring-shaped MCM2-7 hexamer with bound Cdt1 to DNA, and then loads a second MCM2-7 hexamer in a head-to-head orientation, whereby this double hexamer is topologically linked to double-stranded DNA (reviewed in [O'Donnell et al., 2013; Siddiqui et al., 2013; Bell and Labib, 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: MCM2-7 double hexamers mark the location of potential origins of DNA replication that can be activated during S phase to replicate the genome.
source: These MCM2-7 double hexamers mark the location of potential origins of DNA replication that can be activated during S phase to replicate the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCM2-7 function.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the pre-RC includes the two head-to-head associated Mcm2-7 hexamers with each hexamer destined to become a part of the Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) helicase at each replication fork during S phase.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the pre-RC includes the two head-to-head associated Mcm2-7 hexamers with each hexamer destined to become a part of the Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) helicase at each replication fork during S phase (Abid Ali and Costa, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Regulated assembly and disassembly of the pre-RC ensures that the genome replicates only once during each cell division cycle.
source: Regulated assembly and disassembly of the pre-RC ensures that the genome replicates only once during each cell division cycle (O'Donnell et al., 2013; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In budding yeasts, ORC is a stable complex consisting of five AAA+ related subunits and another subunit, Orc6.
source: In budding yeasts, ORC is a stable complex consisting of five AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) related subunits and another subunit, Orc6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast ORC composition.

claim: Orc1, Orc4 and Orc5 are bona-fide members of a large class of AAA+ proteins that contain the characteristic Walker-A and Walker-B motifs.
source: Orc1, Orc4 and Orc5 are bona-fide members of a large class of AAA+ proteins that contain the characteristic Walker-A and Walker-B motifs, but the only active ATPase in S. cerevisiae ORC is the Orc1 subunit with its adjacent Orc4 subunit that contributes an activating arginine finger and other residues required for ORC function in vivo (Loo et al., 1995; Klemm et al., 1997; Bowers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The only active ATPase in S. cerevisiae ORC is the Orc1 subunit with its adjacent Orc4 subunit that contributes an activating arginine finger and other residues required for ORC function in vivo.
source: Orc1, Orc4 and Orc5 are bona-fide members of a large class of AAA+ proteins that contain the characteristic Walker-A and Walker-B motifs, but the only active ATPase in S. cerevisiae ORC is the Orc1 subunit with its adjacent Orc4 subunit that contributes an activating arginine finger and other residues required for ORC function in vivo (Loo et al., 1995; Klemm et al., 1997; Bowers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in the Walker-A motif of S. cerevisiae Orc4 and Orc5 are not essential for cell proliferation.
source: Mutations in the Walker-A motif of S. cerevisiae Orc4 and Orc5 are not essential for cell proliferation (Loo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Orc2 and Orc3 were predicted to contain an AAA+ fold, but these subunits do not have the residues that are important for ATP hydrolysis and thus are predicted to be 'AAA+ like'.
source: Moreover, Orc2 and Orc3 were predicted to contain an AAA+ fold, but these subunits do not have the residues that are important for ATP hydrolysis and thus are predicted to be 'AAA+ like' (Bell et al., 1993; Foss and Rine, 1993; Micklem et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The yeast ORC binds to origin DNA throughout the cell division cycle, even during mitotic exit.
source: The yeast ORC binds to origin DNA throughout the cell division cycle, even during mitotic exit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast ORC behavior.

claim: During G1 phase, yeast ORC recruits the Orc1-related initiator protein Cdc6, another AAA+ ATPase, to the origin DNA, creating an extended footprint over the entire origin.
source: During G1 phase, it recruits the Orc1-related initiator protein Cdc6, another AAA+ ATPase, to the origin DNA, creating an extended footprint over the entire origin (Diffley et al., 1994; Liang et al., 1995; Speck et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In human cells, ORC binding to chromosomes is dynamic, with the first step being the binding of ORC1 to mitotic chromosomes and the subsequent assembly of ORC onto chromatin during the next G1 phase.
source: In contrast, in human cells, ORC binding to chromosomes is dynamic, with the first step being the binding of ORC1 to mitotic chromosomes and the subsequent assembly of ORC onto chromatin during the next G1 phase (Okuno et al., 2001; Siddiqui and Stillman, 2007; Wu et al., 2014; Kara et al., 2015; Abid Ali and Costa, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: During entry into S phase, the human ORC1 subunit is degraded.
source: During entry into S phase, the human ORC1 subunit is degraded (reviewed in [DePamphilis 2003]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Several low-resolution structures of ORC from Drosophila melanogaster and Saccharomyces cerevisiae are available, but they show different architectures.
source: Several low-resolution structures of ORC from Drosophila melanogaster (Clarey et al., 2006; Bleichert et al., 2013) and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Speck et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012) are available, but they show different architectures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: A high-resolution crystal structure of the Drosophila melanogaster ORC (DmORC) was reported.
source: Recently, a high-resolution crystal structure of the Drosophila melanogaster ORC (DmORC) was reported (Bleichert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The DmORC structure contains truncated versions of ORC1, ORC2, and ORC3, full-length ORC4 and ORC5, and a small fragment of ORC6.
source: This structure contains truncated versions of ORC1, ORC2, and ORC3, full-length ORC4 and ORC5, and a small fragment of ORC6.
evidence: This describes the composition of the DmORC structure from the cited study.

claim: The overall shape of the DmORC crystal structure matches the shape observed in the low-resolution EM structures of this complex.
source: The overall shape of the crystal structure matches the shape observed in the low-resolution EM structures of this complex.
evidence: This is a comparison between different structural studies.

claim: The DmORC was captured in a state that is inactive for ATP hydrolysis by ORC1, the most critical ATPase subunit.
source: The DmORC was captured in a state that is inactive for ATP hydrolysis by ORC1, the most critical ATPase subunit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DmORC structure.

claim: In the DmORC structure, the interface between ORC1 and ORC4 and thus the ATP-binding site is disrupted, even though one of the crystal forms reported bound nucleotide.
source: This is because the interface between ORC1 and ORC4 and thus the ATP-binding site is disrupted, even though one of the crystal forms reported bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is an observation about the DmORC structure.

claim: The DmORC state would have to undergo a substantial conformational transition in order to become functionally active for ATP hydrolysis.
source: This state of the complex would have to undergo a substantial conformational transition in order to become functionally active for ATP hydrolysis, as noted by the authors.
evidence: This is an interpretation noted by the authors of the DmORC structure.

claim: The structure of human ORC is in a functionally active, ATP-hydrolysis ready state.
source: Here, we report the structure of human ORC in a functionally active, ATP-hydrolysis ready state, providing insight into ATP-dependent protein loading as well as DNA and CDC6 binding.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the structure determined in this study.

claim: Meier-Gorlin Syndrome is a primordial dwarfism, microcephalic disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding pre-replicative complex proteins, including ORC1, ORC4, ORC6 and CDC6.
source: Meier-Gorlin Syndrome is a primordial dwarfism, microcephalic disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding pre-replicative complex proteins, including ORC1, ORC4, ORC6 and CDC6 (Bicknell et al., 2011a, 2011b; Guernsey et al., 2011; de Munnik et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The HsORC particle was separated into two lobes for structural studies, one consisting of an N-terminally truncated ORC1, full-length ORC4 and a C-terminally truncated ORC5.
source: To facilitate structural studies of HsORC, we separated the particle into two lobes, one consisting of an N-terminally truncated ORC1, full-length ORC4 and a C-terminally truncated ORC5 (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The other lobe of HsORC consists of N-terminally truncated ORC2 and full-length ORC3.
source: The other lobe consists of N-terminally truncated ORC2 and full-length ORC3.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Both HsORC subcomplexes yielded crystals, with the ORC1/4/5 motor module diffracting well to 3.4 Å, and the ORC2/3 subcomplex to 6 Å.
source: Both subcomplexes yielded crystals, with the ORC1/4/5 motor module diffracting well to 3.4 Å, and the ORC2/3 subcomplex to 6 Å (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes the crystallographic results.

claim: The inclusion of ATP was critical to maintain the integrity of the ORC1/4/5 motor module during purification and crystallization.
source: Since ORC1/4/5 is comprised of the active ATPase subunits, the inclusion of ATP was critical to maintain its integrity during purification and crystallization.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: HsORC2/3 is composed of AAA+-like subunits, but with no predicted ATPase activity.
source: In contrast, HsORC2/3 is composed of AAA+-like subunits, but with no predicted ATPase activity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural knowledge.

claim: The two HsORC subcomplexes were modeled into a 20 Å cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) 3D-reconstruction map to obtain a structural model for the HsORC1-5 complex.
source: The two subcomplexes were modeled into a 20 Å cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) 3D-reconstruction map to obtain a structural model for the HsORC1-5 complex.
evidence: This describes the method used to obtain the full complex structure.

claim: The structure of HsORC reveals a remarkable similarity between two very different ATPases: the replication initiator ORC-CDC6 ATPase and the replication fork DNA polymerase clamp loader.
source: The structure of HsORC reveals a remarkable similarity between two very different ATPases: the replication initiator ORC-CDC6 ATPase and the replication fork DNA polymerase clamp loader (Kelch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a structural comparison and interpretation.

claim: Both ORC-CDC6 and DNA polymerase clamp loader ATPases function at different times during genome replication but load ring-shaped proteins onto double-stranded DNA so that the ring-shaped proteins become topologically linked to the DNA double helix.
source: Both ATPases function at different times during genome replication but load ring-shaped proteins onto double-stranded DNA so that the ring-shaped proteins become topologically linked to the DNA double helix.
evidence: This is a functional comparison based on established knowledge.

claim: The structure of the HsORC motor module was solved by molecular replacement using the DmORC4, DmORC5-AAA+ domain and DmORC1-WHD of the DmORC complex as a search model.
source: The structure of the HsORC motor module was solved by molecular replacement using the DmORC4, DmORC5-AAA+ domain and DmORC1-WHD of the DmORC complex (Bleichert et al., 2015) as a search model.
evidence: This describes the crystallographic method used.

claim: The overall architecture of the HsORC motor module resembles a cashew nut.
source: The overall architecture of the HsORC motor module resembles a cashew nut (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a descriptive observation of the structure shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Each ORC subunit in the motor module is comprised of three domains – the RecA-fold, the α-helical lid and the α-helical winged-helix domain (WHD), although the WHD domain was truncated in ORC5.
source: Each ORC subunit is comprised of three domains – the RecA-fold, the α-helical lid and the α-helical winged-helix domain (WHD), although the WHD domain was truncated in ORC5.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: The RecA-fold domain and the lid together constitute the well-known AAA+ domain.
source: The RecA-fold domain and the lid together constitute the well-known AAA+ domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AAA+ domain architecture.

claim: The three RecA domains of the HsORC motor module form a semicircle with ATP nucleotides wedged between them in a classic AAA+ oligomerization arrangement.
source: The three RecA domains form a semicircle with ATP nucleotides wedged between them in a classic AAA+ oligomerization arrangement (see below).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: The RecA and lid domains of ORC1 contact the RecA domain of ORC4 as if cupping that domain between the two.
source: The RecA and lid domains of ORC1 contact the RecA domain of ORC4 as if cupping that domain between the two.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: The RecA and lid domains of ORC4 cup the RecA domain of ORC5.
source: The same is true for the RecA and lid domains of ORC4 cupping the RecA domain of ORC5.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the determined structure.

claim: The three ORC subunits in the motor module have the exact same organization of the three domains with respect to each other and can be readily superimposed.
source: Remarkably, the three ORC subunits have the exact same organization of the three domains with respect to each other and can be readily superimposed (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The domains of the HsORC motor module arrange themselves into a right-handed helical architecture with a ~52° rotation and 2 Å rise.
source: The domains arrange themselves into a right-handed helical architecture with a ~52° rotation and 2 Å rise (58° rotation with a 2.05 Å rise from the AAA+ of ORC1 to ORC4; and 46° rotation with a 2.3 Å rise from the AAA+ of ORC4 to ORC5).
evidence: This is a structural measurement from the determined structure.

claim: The ATPase motor module of HsORC is very reminiscent of the DNA polymerase clamp loader complexes such as Replication Factor C (RFC) in eukaryotes, the bacterial γ-complex, and the T4 bacteriophage Gene44 clamp loader.
source: The ATPase motor module of HsORC is very reminiscent of the DNA polymerase clamp loader complexes such as Replication Factor C (RFC) in eukaryotes, the bacterial γ-complex, and the T4 bacteriophage Gene44 clamp loader (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both the architecture of the subunits and the organization of the domains with respect to each other are remarkably similar between HsORC and clamp loaders, although HsORC is somewhat shallower.
source: Both the architecture of the subunits and the organization of the domains with respect to each other are remarkably similar, although HsORC is somewhat shallower.
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: The rotations between subunits for several clamp loaders range between 56° and 74° with rises in the range of 2.8 to 8.0 Å, excluding a couple of outliers that appear to be in an inactive conformation.
source: The rotations between subunits for several clamp loaders range between 56° and 74° with rises in the range of 2.8 to 8.0 Å, excluding a couple of outliers that appear to be in an inactive conformation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of known clamp loader structures.

claim: Clamp loaders are ATPases that perform a single ATPase cycle to pry open a closed DNA polymerase clamp ring in order to load it onto the double helix of DNA.
source: The clamp loaders are ATPases that perform a single ATPase cycle to pry open a closed DNA polymerase clamp ring in order to load it onto the double helix of DNA (Kelch et al., 2012; Hedglin et al., 2013), in contrast to the continuously hydrolyzing AAA+ helicases (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In the case of HsORC, there is also a single ATPase event, either for loading of the double hexamer of MCM2-7 or for resetting the system.
source: In the case of HsORC, there is also a single ATPase event, either for loading of the double hexamer of MCM2-7 or for resetting the system (Frigola et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The HsORC motor module crystallized with ATP, and the nucleotides can be clearly seen in difference electron-density maps between the subunit interface of ORC1/ORC4 and between the interface ORC4/ORC5, as well as on the surface of ORC5.
source: The HsORC motor module crystallized with ATP, and the nucleotides can be clearly seen in difference electron-density maps between the subunit interface of ORC1/ORC4 and between the interface ORC4/ORC5, as well as on the surface of ORC5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a crystallographic observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Despite the ATPase function of the HsORC motor module, the electron density indicates that ATP hydrolysis had not occurred.
source: Despite the ATPase function of the HsORC motor module, the electron density indicates that ATP hydrolysis had not occurred.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the crystallographic data.

claim: The crystals of the HsORC motor module appeared in less than a day and reproducibly disappeared after an additional day if not promptly harvested and frozen.
source: We note that the crystals appeared in less than a day and reproducibly disappeared after an additional day if not promptly harvested and frozen.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The conformation and placement of the three nucleotides in the HsORC motor module is quite similar, apart from a rotation of the adenine base with respect to the sugar and the absence of an additional subunit that would complete the binding site for ATP in ORC5.
source: The conformation and placement of the three nucleotides is also quite similar, apart from a rotation of the adenine base with respect to the sugar (the angle of the glycosidic bond) and the absence of an additional subunit that would complete the binding site for ATP in ORC5 (see below).
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by ORC is required for replication in vivo.
source: As mentioned earlier, ATP hydrolysis by ORC is required for replication in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The nucleotide-binding sites in HsORC are characteristic of AAA+ ATPases of this family.
source: The nucleotide-binding sites are characteristic of AAA+ ATPases of this family (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Hauk and Berger, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: For the nucleotides at the subunit interfaces in HsORC, Walker-A (P-loop) and Walker-B motifs from the RecA domain of one subunit line one side of the ATP nucleotide and three basic residues line the other side.
source: For the nucleotides at the subunit interfaces: Walker-A (P-loop) and Walker-B motifs from the RecA domain of one subunit line one side of the ATP nucleotide and three basic residues line the other side (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The first basic residue at the ATP-binding site, the 'trigger', is the sensor-2 residue.
source: The first basic residue, the 'trigger', is the sensor-2 residue.
evidence: This is a structural and functional designation.

claim: The trigger residue is ORC1-R720 for the first (ORC1-ORC4) interface and ORC4-R277 for the second (ORC4-ORC5) interface.
source: Specifically, it is ORC1-R720 for the first (ORC1-ORC4) interface and ORC4-R277 for the second (ORC4-ORC5) interface.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The trigger emanates from the lid domain of the subunit that contributes the Walker-A and -B residues to the binding site and is most similar to the F1-ATPase arginine finger.
source: The trigger emanates from the lid domain of the subunit that contributes the Walker-A and -B residues to the binding site and is most similar to the F1-ATPase arginine finger (Kagawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by a citation.

claim: The trigger is what differentiates an ATP-bound and ATP-hydrolyzing configuration.
source: The trigger is what differentiates an ATP-bound and ATP-hydrolyzing configuration.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on structural knowledge.

claim: The precise positioning of the trigger residue appears to regulate the reactivity of the ATP-binding site, with the ATP-hydrolyzing configuration stabilizing the hydrolysis transition state.
source: The precise positioning of this residue appears to regulate the reactivity of the site, with the ATP-hydrolyzing configuration stabilizing the hydrolysis transition state (Kagawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: In ATPases that function continuously, such as helicases, the trigger usually resides on the neighboring subunit to the one harboring the Walker-A and -B motifs.
source: In ATPases that function continuously, such as helicases, the trigger usually resides on the neighboring subunit to the one harboring the Walker-A and -B motifs, whereas in ATPases such as ORC, and the clamp loader RFC, where there is probably a single hydrolysis event, the trigger resides on the same subunit (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: In ATPases such as ORC and the clamp loader RFC, where there is probably a single hydrolysis event, the trigger resides on the same subunit.
source: In ATPases that function continuously, such as helicases, the trigger usually resides on the neighboring subunit to the one harboring the Walker-A and -B motifs, whereas in ATPases such as ORC, and the clamp loader RFC, where there is probably a single hydrolysis event, the trigger resides on the same subunit (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Factors that interact with the lid domain may have a profound effect on the positioning of the lid domain and therefore the trigger and consequently on the activation of ORC ATPase activity.
source: Factors that interact with the lid domain may have a profound effect on the positioning of the lid domain and therefore the trigger and consequently on the activation of ORC ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural insights.

claim: The ORC1 trigger residue is mutated in a Meier-Gorlin Syndrome (MGS) patient (ORC1-R720Q) who also carries a mutation (ORC1-R105Q) in the amino-terminus that disrupts ORC1's Cyclin E-CDK2 inhibitory activity and histone H4K20me2 binding.
source: Interestingly, the ORC1 trigger residue is mutated in a Meier-Gorlin Syndrome (MGS) patient (ORC1-R720Q) who also carries a mutation (ORC1-R105Q) in the amino-terminus that disrupts ORC1's Cyclin E-CDK2 inhibitory activity and histone H4K20me2 binding (Hossain and Stillman, 2012; Kuo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: MGS patients with ORC1 mutations display the most severe phenotype of short stature and microcephaly.
source: MGS patients with ORC1 mutations display the most severe phenotype of short stature and microcephaly (de Munnik et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The second basic residue opposite the P-loop is commonly referred to as the R-finger in the AAA+ family and functions as the 'piston', since it moves in and out of the site based on the presence of the γ-phosphate of the nucleotide.
source: The second basic residue opposite the P-loop is commonly referred to as the R-finger in the AAA+ family and functions as the 'piston', since it moves in and out of the site based on the presence of the γ-phosphate of the nucleotide (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The R-finger (piston) is ORC4-R209 at the first interface and ORC5-R143 at the second interface.
source: It is ORC4-R209 at the first interface and ORC5-R143 at the second interface.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The third basic residue, the 'tether', forms contacts between the R-finger side of the interface to the Walker-A, -B side.
source: The third basic residue, the 'tether', forms contacts between the R-finger side of the interface to the Walker-A, -B side.
evidence: This is a structural and functional designation.

claim: ORC4-R205 performs the tether function at the first interface as it contacts the Walker-B residue E621 as well as D623 of ORC1.
source: ORC4-R205 performs this function at the first interface as it contacts the Walker-B residue E621 as well as D623 of ORC1.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: A second tether is formed by ORC4-Y174, which interacts with ORC1-E621.
source: However, a second tether is formed by ORC4-Y174, which interacts with ORC1-E621 as well.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: ORC4-Y174 is mutated in three MGS patients (ORC4-Y174C) and is conserved in all ORC4 subunits from yeast to mammals.
source: ORC4-Y174 is also mutated in three MGS patients (ORC4-Y174C) and is conserved in all ORC4 subunits from yeast to mammals.
evidence: This is based on patient data and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: In addition to the well-known R-finger, ORC4-Y174 plays a critical role in sensing the nucleotide state at the ORC1-ORC4 interface.
source: We suggest that in addition to the well-known R-finger, this tyrosine plays a critical role in sensing the nucleotide state at this critical interface.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural observations.

claim: A tyrosine exists at a comparable position in ORC1 (ORC1-Y634) that is highly conserved, but a proline occupies that position in ORC5 (ORC5-P139).
source: Indeed, a tyrosine exists at a comparable position in ORC1 (ORC1-Y634) that is highly conserved, but a proline occupies that position in ORC5 (ORC5-P139).
evidence: This is a structural observation and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: ORC1-Y634 is predicted to interact with the CDC6 Walker-B motif (CDC6-E285) in a similar fashion to ORC4-Y174.
source: We predict that ORC1-Y634 interacts with the CDC6 Walker-B motif (CDC6-E285) in a similar fashion (see below).
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural analogy.

claim: At the second P-loop interface between ORC4 and ORC5, ORC5-R104 is identified as the tether as it forms a salt bridge with ORC4-E113.
source: At the second P-loop interface between ORC4 and ORC5, we identify ORC5-R104 as the tether as it forms a salt bridge with ORC4-E113.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: One distinct feature of the Walker-A motif in ORC4 is the presence of an arginine, R69, in the center of the loop.
source: One distinct feature of the Walker-A motif (P-loop) in ORC4 is the presence of an arginine, R69, in the center of the loop (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 3b.

claim: ORC4-R69 is completely conserved in mammals, avian, fish and anthropods.
source: It is completely conserved in mammals, avian, fish and anthropods.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: ORC4-R69 forms a salt bridge with ORC4-E160 of the Walker-B motif.
source: It forms a salt bridge with ORC4-E160 of the Walker-B motif.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: ORC4-R69 is also present in the tau subunit of the E. coli clamp loader.
source: It is also present in the tau subunit of the E. coli clamp loader.
